newsitem.title: USA: Fox aims to compete with Disney in animated films.
newsitem.headline: Fox aims to compete with Disney in animated films.

text.p: Move over, Mickey Mouse. Rupert Murdoch's Twentieth Century Fox studio is looking to muscle in on one of Walt Disney Co.'s prized possessions -- animated feature films.

Armed with a state-of-the-art animation studio here, Fox is preparing to fire its first salvo later this year with the release of "Anastasia," based on the legendary Russian princess of the same name.
Fox is not alone. DreamWorks SKG, Paramount and Warner Bros. all have animated features in production for release in 1998.
However, Hal Vogel, an analyst with Cowen & Co. of New York, who closely follows Disney, said the Hollywood giant should have no immediate worries about the growing competition.

"A lot of people have tried (competing against Disney in animated feature films) and most have failed ... because Disney is so efficient at production and distribution and marketing of the animated feature that they've got it down to a science," Vogel said. He added that he expects the competition to "take chips off the market share but not grab a dominant amount."

Vogel also noted that despite the marketing clout of the other big studios, Disney had a special niche in home video sales that the others did not. "Disney really knows how to market (animated features on home video) better than anybody else," he said.
"Anastasia," almost three years in the making, is being produced at Fox's new animation studio under the watchful eyes of co-producers and directors Don Bluth and Gary Goldman.
Ironically, the Fox production is being overseen by three former Disney executives: Bill Mechanic, recently named head of Fox Studios, Bluth and Goldman.

The latter two owned their own production company, based in Dublin, Ireland, which was responsible for such animated features as "Land Before Time," "All Dogs Go to Heaven," "Thumbelina" and "A Troll in Central Park."

While their products all ranked in the top 15 of first-run animated features, their box office revenues paled in comparison to Disney's mega-hits. When Fox asked them to join its new animation unit, they jumped at the chance.
During a recent tour of the Fox Animation Studio, Bluth said his main reason for joining Fox was that the company had the strength to tackle Disney on its own turf.
He said the major studios started establishing their own animation departments four years ago.

"When those giants jumped into the animation ring, all the little independent producers really had only two choices; get clobbered or get out of the ring. So I think at that point Gary and I decided that what we needed to do was team up with one of the giants, and that's why we went with Fox," Bluth said.
Michael Malone, Fox's senior vice president of licensing and merchandising, said recently that Fox would promote "Anastasia" "more aggressively" than any other film in the studio's history.
The promotion will include a partnership with Burger King -- the first time the fast-food giant has made such a deal with a studio other than Disney.
Burger King is one of the 43 licensees that will merchandise "Anastasia" toys, dolls and other spin-offs, including apparel, publishing, housewares and toiletries.
Fox plans to release an animated feature once every 18 months, the next being "Planet Ice," a science fiction adventure planned for release in late 1998 or early 1999.
Goldman said he did not expect Disney to lie down under the onslaught of competition.

Asked why independent animation producers had failed to dent Disney's supremacy, he said: "Strictly in my opinion, I'd say Disney doesn't want anybody else to succeed in animated films; if you go up against them, you've got a formidable opponent."
He said Disney has in the past put its mega-hits out at the same time as independents have released their products.

"I don't know exactly how it works. I just know that when we've come out in the past, they've come out with all guns blazing. They'll figure out when you're going to release ... and you'll find three of their top movies up against you and then you're hunting for theatres because theatre owners know (Disney films) are winners.
"When we came out with "All Dogs Go to Heaven," Disney came out with "Little Mermaid" and we got hammered," Goldman said.
He said Fox's strategy will be to "weave itself in and out of the competition ... and not be in a head-to-head situation."
To that end, Fox plans to release "Anastasia" in late November, avoiding a clash with Disney's "Hercules," slated for summer release.

Fox describes "Anastasia" as a "20th-century fairy tale" based on the myth and mystery surrounding Anastasia, the lost Russian Princess who some believe was the only member of the ruling Romanov family to survive the Russian revolution.
